Gladly. Here's a subject I keep coming back to: the price of light.

**The Price of Light**

Nobody threw a festival when light became cheap. No parade, no plaque — which is a shame, because the collapse in the price of light may be one of the largest economic events in human history. The economist William Nordhaus once tried to measure it, comparing the labor it took to make light in ancient Babylon with the labor it takes now. A Babylonian worked roughly a week to earn the light a modern bulb pours out in a single hour; we earn that hour with a second or two of work. The collapse was so complete that ordinary price statistics barely register it — which was Nordhaus's point: measured conventionally, we look only modestly richer than people who couldn't afford to read after sunset.

For most of human history, light was astonishingly expensive, and darkness governed the schedule. Families rose with the sun not out of virtue but economics. Candles were a purchase of real weight: the tallow kind were made of rendered animal fat and smoked and stank accordingly, while beeswax burned clean and was priced accordingly. The brightness of your home advertised your income. Poor households owned one candle, or none, and children learned their letters by hearth-glow — Abraham Lincoln did his boyhood reading by firelight. The sperm whale was hunted across whole oceans in part so that wealthy drawing rooms could burn clean, bright candles. Light had a body count.

The expense of illumination even shaped sleep. The historian A. Roger Ekirch, digging through centuries of diaries, court records, and medical texts, found that pre-industrial Europeans slept in two shifts: a "first sleep," then an hour or two of wakefulness in the dark middle of the night, then a "second sleep." People used the interval to pray, to talk, to interpret dreams, to visit neighbors; one sixteenth-century French physician even advised couples that conception was likeliest after the first sleep. And what sounds exotic turns out to be dormant rather than extinct. When the researcher Thomas Wehr confined volunteers to long, pre-electric nights, their sleep split into the same two blocks within weeks. The old darkness is still in us, waiting.

Then we started to win. Gas came first — London's Pall Mall became the first gaslit street in 1807 — and the night acquired a luminous edge. Lamplighting became a profession; nightlife became a possibility. Electricity finished the job: Edison's practical bulb arrived in 1879, his Pearl Street station lit lower Manhattan in 1882, and at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, Westinghouse strung roughly a hundred thousand bulbs across the White City, which visitors described in frankly religious terms. Light stopped being a tool and became an ideology. "Enlightenment" was already a metaphor; now it was a municipal budget line. Cities competed in brightness, and from orbit tonight you can read the winners.

But every conquest sends a bill, and this one arrived late. In 2016, astronomers published a world atlas of artificial sky brightness and reported that a third of humanity — including most North Americans and Europeans — can no longer see the Milky Way. The stars, our species' oldest shared text, its first calendar, clock, and map, have gone out of print. Our bodies, still built for the old regime, keep filing complaints: the light that leaks into modern evenings is rich in exactly the blue wavelengths fire never produced, the wavelengths our retinas read as morning, and so melatonin quietly withdraws. Sea turtle hatchlings, evolved to find the ocean by crawling toward the moon-bright horizon, crawl inland toward porch lights. Moths spiral into lamps by the billions. Migrating birds tangle in the glow of tall buildings. After the 1994 Northridge earthquake knocked out Los Angeles's power, officials reportedly fielded calls about a strange silvery cloud hanging over the city. The Milky Way had come back.

Which is how the circle closes in a way no Babylonian would believe: darkness has become a luxury good. We buy blackout curtains. Hotels advertise their darkness. There are whole parks certified for the quality of their night skies, and people drive for hours to stand under the Milky Way — many of them, guides report, seeing it properly for the first time in their lives, and some of them weeping. We spent thousands of years buying our way out of the night, and now we pay to visit it.

I don't think we chose badly. Electric light is unambiguously one of the great goods: surgeries at midnight, children reading past sunset, streets where walking at night no longer means taking your life in your hands. (Night really was dangerous; "curfew" descends from *couvre-feu*, the medieval order to bank your fire, flame being the terror of cities built of wood.) The lesson seems subtler: when something becomes nearly free, we stop noticing we're spending it. Light used to be rationed by price, and the rationing, whatever its miseries, gave shape to time — first sleep and second sleep, the storytelling hour, a built-in daily encounter with our own smallness under a vast sky. Our bright nights have a shape too, but it is the shape of an endless afternoon.

Maybe darkness deserves the same conservation we grant rivers and forests — not because it is useful, though it turns out it is, but because it is inheritance: the one spectacle every human before us saw without owning it. A Babylonian worked a week for a single bulb-hour of brightness; we burn that before breakfast and forget to look up. Somewhere between those two economies lies a balance, and finding it may be the next chapter in the history of light: learning, at last, to see in the dark.

---

**The Price of Light**

Nobody threw a festival when light became cheap. There was no parade and no plaque, which is a shame, because the collapse in the price of light may be one of the largest economic events in human history. The economist William Nordhaus tried once to measure it: comparing the labor it took to make light in ancient Babylon with the labor it takes now, he estimated that light has become tens of thousands of times cheaper. A Babylonian worked roughly a week to earn the light a modern bulb pours out in a single hour; we earn that hour with a second or two of work. Whole orders of magnitude were erased, one wick, filament, and diode at a time. And because price indexes mostly failed to notice, official statistics still imply we're only modestly richer than people who couldn't afford to read after sunset.

Because that's the thing we forget: for most of human history, light was astonishingly expensive, and darkness governed the schedule. Families rose with the sun not out of virtue but economics. Candles were a purchase of real weight; the tallow kind were made of rendered animal fat and smoked and stank accordingly, while beeswax burned clean and was priced accordingly. The brightness of your home advertised your income. Poor households owned one candle, or none, and children learned their letters by hearth-glow if they learned them at all. The sperm whale was hunted across whole oceans in part so that wealthy drawing rooms could burn clean, bright candles. Light had a body count.

The expense of illumination even shaped sleep itself. The historian A. Roger Ekirch, digging through centuries of diaries, court records, and medical texts, found that pre-industrial Europeans slept in two shifts: a "first sleep," then an hour or two of wakefulness in the dark middle of the night, then a "second sleep." People used the interval to pray, to talk, to interpret dreams, to visit neighbors; one sixteenth-century French physician even advised couples that conception was likeliest after the first sleep. And what sounds exotic turns out to be dormant rather than extinct. When the sleep researcher Thomas Wehr confined volunteers to long, pre-electric nights, their sleep split into the same two blocks within a few weeks. The old darkness is still in us, waiting.

Then we started to win. Gas came first - London's Pall Mall became the first gaslit street in 1807 - and the night acquired a luminous edge. Lamplighting became a profession; nightlife became a possibility. Electricity finished the job. Edison's practical bulb arrived in 1879, his Pearl Street station lit lower Manhattan in 1882, and at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, Westinghouse strung roughly a hundred thousand bulbs across the White City, which visitors described in frankly religious terms. Light stopped being a tool and became an ideology. "Enlightenment" was already a metaphor; now it was a municipal budget line. Cities competed in brightness, and from orbit tonight you can read the winners.

But every conquest sends a bill, and this one arrived late. In 2016, astronomers published a world atlas of artificial sky brightness and reported that a third of humanity - including most North Americans and Europeans - can no longer see the Milky Way. The stars, our species' oldest shared text, its first calendar, clock, and map, have gone out of print. Our bodies, still built for the old regime, keep filing complaints: the light that leaks into modern evenings is rich in exactly the blue wavelengths that fire never produced, the wavelengths our retinas read as morning, and so melatonin quietly withdraws. Sea turtle hatchlings, evolved to find the ocean by crawling toward the moon-bright horizon, crawl inland toward porch lights. Moths spiral into lamps by the billions. Migrating birds get tangled in the glow of tall buildings.

Which is how the circle closes in a way no Babylonian would believe: darkness has become a luxury good. We buy blackout curtains. Hotels advertise their darkness. There are parks certified by an international body for the quality of their night skies, and people drive for hours to stand under the Milky Way - many of them, guides report, seeing it properly for the first time in their lives, and some of them weeping. We spent thousands of years - most of our history - buying our way out of the night, and now we pay to visit it.

I don't think we chose badly. Electric light is unambiguously one of the great goods: surgeries at midnight, children reading past sunset, streets where walking at night no longer means taking your life in your hands. (Night really was dangerous; "curfew" descends from couvre-feu, the medieval order to bank your fire, because flame was the terror of cities built of wood.) The lesson seems subtler. When something becomes nearly free, we stop noticing that we're spending it. Light used to be rationed by price, and the rationing, whatever its miseries, gave shape to time - first sleep and second sleep, the storytelling hour, a built-in daily encounter with our own smallness under a vast sky. Our bright nights have a shape too, but it is the shape of an endless afternoon.

Maybe darkness deserves the same conservation we grant rivers and forests - not because it is useful, though it turns out it is, but because it is inheritance: the one spectacle every human before us saw without owning it. The Babylonian lamp returned minutes of glow for hours of labor. We flood whole cities all night and have forgotten to look up. Somewhere between those two economies lies a balance, and finding it may be the next chapter in the long history of light: learning, at last, to see in the dark.
